why_this_tool: Kubernetes ships the isolation, quota, priority and network primitives that every multi-tenant ML platform is built from, so practising them directly shows what the higher-level tools add.
alternatives: Kueue and Volcano add job queueing and fair-share batch scheduling on top of the cluster, vCluster gives each tenant a virtual control plane instead of a namespace, gVisor sandboxes untrusted containers at the runtime layer, Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper enforce tenant policy at admission, and Envoy applies rate limits and load shedding at the request layer.

setup.do: Install a container runtime, kubectl and a local multi-node cluster tool such as kind or minikube, and start a cluster with one control plane node and two workers, using a network plugin that enforces NetworkPolicy.
setup.done_when: kubectl lists three Ready nodes and the network plugin pods are Running in the system namespace.
setup.why: NetworkPolicy objects are silently ignored when the network plugin does not implement them, so tenant network isolation cannot be practised on a default plugin that lacks support.

setup.do: Confirm that the ResourceQuota admission controller is enabled on the API server of your local cluster.
setup.done_when: The API server admission plugin list, or its default set, includes ResourceQuota.
setup.why: Quota is enforced at admission time, so if the plugin is off every quota you create later is recorded but never enforced.

setup.do: List the initial namespaces of the cluster and set a namespace preference in your kubectl context so you can switch between tenants quickly.
setup.done_when: kubectl shows the initial namespaces and your current context reports the namespace you set.
setup.why: Every later step is scoped to a tenant namespace, and a wrong default namespace is the most common cause of confusing results.

steps.do: Create two tenant namespaces, team-a and team-b, plus a shared platform namespace, and label each with a tenant name, following the namespace per tenant model.
steps.done_when: kubectl lists the three namespaces with their tenant labels, and you can state one case where a virtual control plane per tenant would be needed instead.
steps.why: The namespace is the base unit of control plane isolation, and comparing it with the virtual control plane model tells you when namespaces alone are not enough.

steps.do: Create a ResourceQuota in each tenant namespace that caps total CPU and memory requests and limits, with a larger share for team-a than for team-b.
steps.done_when: Describing the quota in each namespace shows the hard values you set and zero used.
steps.why: A compute quota is how a platform turns scarce shared capacity into a predictable per-tenant share.

steps.do: Run a pod without resource requests in team-a, then a deployment sized to exceed the team-b quota, and query the quota usage after each attempt.
steps.done_when: The pod without requests is rejected with a quota error, the oversized deployment stalls below its replica count, and the quota shows used close to hard.
steps.why: Seeing admission reject the request is the first form of backpressure a tenant meets, and reading used against hard is how you debug it.

steps.do: Create three PriorityClass objects for low, medium and high priority work and a quota per tenant scoped to each priority class, so only a small share of each tenant budget can run at high priority.
steps.done_when: A high priority pod beyond the scoped quota is rejected while a low priority pod of the same size in the same namespace is admitted.
steps.why: Priority-scoped quota stops one tenant from marking every training job as urgent and starving the others during contention.

steps.do: Apply a default deny policy for all ingress and egress in both tenant namespaces, then add a policy that allows traffic only from pods in the same namespace and from the platform namespace.
steps.done_when: A request from a team-a pod to a team-b pod times out, while a request between two team-a pods succeeds.

verified.section_found: Default deny all ingress and all egress traffic

steps.why: Namespaces do not isolate network traffic by themselves, so data plane isolation between tenants needs an explicit deny by default.

steps.do: Configure node isolation by tainting and labelling one worker for team-a only, and run a team-a pod with the matching toleration and node selector next to a team-b pod without them.
steps.done_when: The team-a pod lands on the dedicated worker and the team-b pod is never scheduled there.
steps.why: Dedicated nodes are the stronger and more expensive isolation layer, used for noisy or sensitive workloads such as accelerator training.

steps.do: Create a quota on an extended resource name in team-b to stand in for accelerators, since a laptop has no GPU, and compare the sum of all tenant quotas with the allocatable capacity of your nodes.
steps.done_when: You have a small table per tenant of quota hard, quota used and share of node allocatable, and can say whether the cluster is overcommitted.
steps.why: Quota is independent of real capacity, so the gap between promised quota and actual nodes is the overcommit trade-off you attribute and charge back per tenant.

steps.do: Create a Service with the same name in team-a and team-b, then query its short name and its fully qualified name from a pod in each namespace and compare the answers.
steps.done_when: The short name resolves to the local tenant Service in each namespace, and the fully qualified name of the other tenant resolves but the connection is blocked.

source.title: DNS for Services and Pods | Kubernetes

steps.why: DNS is shared across tenants, so you need to see exactly what a tenant can discover by name even when network policy blocks the traffic.

steps.do: Deploy a shared model serving Service in the platform namespace with a readiness probe, make one replica fail readiness to simulate overload, and query the EndpointSlice conditions while it happens.
steps.done_when: The EndpointSlice shows the failing replica as not ready while the other replicas keep receiving requests from both tenants.
steps.why: Removing an overloaded backend from rotation through the ready and serving conditions is the built-in load shedding signal on a shared service.

steps.do: Read the API Priority and Fairness section and note how flow control keeps one tenant with a busy controller or a job storm from exhausting the API server for everyone.
steps.done_when: You can explain in two sentences how a flood of API requests from one tenant is queued or rejected without blocking the others.
steps.why: Backpressure on the shared control plane is a different mechanism from quota on workloads, and a design review will ask about both.

steps.do: Write a pinned cluster configuration and an admission configuration that limits the high priority class to namespaces holding a matching quota, keep them with all tenant manifests in one repository, then delete the cluster and reproduce it from those files.
steps.done_when: A freshly recreated cluster rejects a high priority pod in a namespace without a matching quota, with no manual step after applying the repository.
steps.why: Tenant onboarding has to be repeatable from version control, and limiting priority classes by default closes the gap where a new namespace has no quota yet.

steps.do: Configure a production-like entry point by installing an ingress controller and creating one Ingress with name based virtual hosting that routes a host per tenant to that tenant's serving Service, with quotas, policies and priority classes all in force.
steps.done_when: Requests with the team-a host reach only team-a pods, requests with the team-b host reach only team-b pods, and scaling one tenant past its quota does not change the response of the other.
steps.why: A real shared platform exposes many tenants behind one edge, and this is where isolation, quota and overload behaviour have to hold together under traffic.
